title: Super choice could be a $230k retirement error
full_text:
Superannuation fund members risk missing out on hundreds of thousands of extra dollars at retirement simply because of how their funds invest their money.
Most of Australia’s super providers still offer a single default strategy, typically a balanced portfolio, for all members despite recent growth of lifecycle investment options, which invest based on your age. This delivers an aggressive growth strategy when younger and a conservative approach when older.
Figures from the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority show that among 42 major superannuation funds, 17 offer lifecycle investing as their default MySuper product.
New modelling by Aware Super found a typical 35-year-old with $89,000 in the median MySuper balance fund will have $867,000 at retirement, while a lifecycle option will grow to $1.095m – a $228,000 difference.
Aware Super head of investment strategy Michael Winchester said research group Chant West had found lifecycle funds outperformed single-option MySuper funds by 0.5 per cent annually over the decade to March 2026.
“If evidence continues to show that lifecycle strategies deliver better retirement outcomes for members, we expect they will become increasingly common across the industry,” he said.
Supporters of the traditional single balanced default strategy say it’s simpler, easier and cheaper to run, and removes the timing risk of switching someone to a more conservative option just as financial markets tank – locking them out of a full rebound.
Lifecycle super supporters say balanced default funds, where up to 30 per cent of members’ money sits in conservative assets such as cash and bonds, do not offer the growth potential for younger people who have decades before retirement and can afford to hold more higher-risk, higher-growth investments such as shares and property.
Mr Winchester said people in their 20s, 30s and 40s were most likely to be affected by sticking with lower-risk balanced funds for their entire careers.
“They generally have the longest investment horizon and the greatest capacity to recover from market downturns, meaning they can benefit most from maintaining a higher exposure to growth assets,” he said.
Lifecycle super is offered mainly by retail funds including AMP, Mercer and Vanguard, although Aware Super, ART and some other industry funds set them as default. Industry giants AustralianSuper, Hostplus, REST, UniSuper, Hesta and Cbus are among those sticking with single default strategy for members.
Each lifecycle product is different, so members should understand the asset allocation and risk level, and how it rebalances as they age.
For example, Aware Super has members invested in 88 per cent growth/12 per cent defensive assets until age 56, then it gradually switches to a 59 per cent growth/41 per cent defensive mix after age 65.
Global investment giant Vanguard’s lifecycle MySuper product uses 90 per cent growth assets until age 47, then gradually rebalances towards a 40 per cent growth/60 per cent defensive mix at age 82.
Dialling up or down Vanguard Asia Pacific chief investment officer Duncan Burns said people just starting their career had very different investment needs to those nearing retirement.
“The challenge is that many people don’t know how much investment risk is appropriate at different stages of life or when they should adjust their asset allocation,” he said.
Lifecycle super did the work for them, Mr Burns said, automatically adjusting their investment mix over time.
“One common issue in superannuation is that younger members often take too little risk, missing out on potential long-term growth, while older members may take on too much risk, exposing their savings to market downturns just when they need stability most,” he said.
“The lifecycle approach aims to strike the right balance, maximising growth potential early on and reducing risk as retirement approaches.” JBS Financial Strategists chief executive Jenny Brown said lifecycle super was potentially good “from a set-and-forget perspective if you don’t engage with your superannuation investments”.
“We often find people who haven’t had advisers come to us in their 40s and they’re automatically conservative in nature, and therefore they want to be conservative in their super investments and are not thinking that it’s long-term,” she said.
“Longer term, you have the passage of time to ride out the lumps, bumps and corrections in the market.” Even people in their 60s should hold growth assets to retain exposure to long-term gains, Ms Brown said.
“Check what the asset allocation is because you don’t want to be really conservative at 60, because you’ve potentially still got 30 years of investing,” she said. “If you have 30 per cent cash inside super and add that to what you’ve got outside super, you can be overall in a very defensive portfolio. It’s worthwhile considering what you’re invested in, in its totality with all your other investments.”
